content: Gliclazide is an oral hypoglycemic agent, classified as a sulfonylurea, and is primarily used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is marketed under the brand name Diamicron MR® and is also distributed under various other names, including Diabeton MR, Diamicron 30 mg, Diamicron LM 30 mg, Diamicron MR 30 mg, Diamicron Uno 30 mg, Dianormax MR, Diaprel MR, and Uni Diamicron. However, it is not available in the United States. Each tablet of gliclazide contains 80 mg of the active ingredient. The drug is indicated for the control of hyperglycemia in patients with stable, mild, non-ketosis-prone, maturity-onset, or adult-type diabetes mellitus. It is prescribed when proper dietary management and exercise fail to achieve glycemic control or when insulin therapy is deemed inappropriate. The recommended dosage ranges from 40 mg to 240 mg daily, depending on the patient’s response. It is typically administered once or twice daily before meals, with a maximum single dose of 160 mg. Gliclazide exerts its hypoglycemic effects by restoring the first-phase insulin secretion and enhancing insulin sensitivity. Additionally, it has glycemia-independent hemovascular effects and antioxidant properties. The drug does not produce active circulating metabolites. Gliclazide is contraindicated in patients with type 1 diabetes, hypersensitivity to sulfonylureas, severe renal or hepatic failure, and during pregnancy or lactation. It is also contraindicated when co-prescribed with miconazole. Drug interactions may occur with gliclazide. Its hypoglycemic action can be diminished by agents such as danazol, chlorpromazine, glucocorticoids, progestogens, and β-2 agonists. Conversely, its hypoglycemic effect may be potentiated by substances like phenylbutazone, alcohol, fluconazole, β-blockers, and possibly ACE inhibitors. Adverse effects associated with gliclazide include hypoglycemia, gastrointestinal disturbances (commonly reported), rare skin reactions, rare hematological disorders, and exceptional cases of hepatic enzyme elevations. In cases of overdose, severe hypoglycemia may occur, necessitating urgent intravenous glucose administration and close monitoring of the patient.
